title: Why I Spend My Time on CEOs
author: Managing the Future
summary: The author — a multi-decade former CEO turned executive coach — explains why he chose to devote his post-operational career to coaching sitting CEOs rather than pursuing advisory boards or the conference circuit. He argues the CEO role is categorically different from all other leadership positions: it combines maximum public exposure with maximum isolation from honest feedback, and most people who land in it do so without a real support system or peer group capable of genuine candor. The article traces a theory of CEO failure rooted not in strategic error but in the accumulated consequences of distorted feedback, isolation, and misaligned board dynamics. He identifies the scale of the opportunity: 200,000 sitting CEOs, each running the most consequential system in their world with no manual. The essay redefines legacy not as retrospective achievement but as the ability to be genuinely useful right now to people navigating hard work.
points: The CEO role is categorically different from all other executive positions — it combines maximum public exposure with maximum isolation from honest feedback.
Most CEO failures are not strategic errors but accumulated consequences of distorted feedback loops that no one in the organisation has the standing to correct.
There are approximately 200,000 sitting CEOs who were handed the most consequential job in their company with no manual and no meaningful support system.
The board circuit and advisory roles offer retrospective validation — coaching sitting CEOs offers the chance to be useful to people in the middle of the hardest work.
Legacy, properly understood, is not about past achievement — it is about whether you are still genuinely useful right now to people who need you most.
quotes: Not because the world needs another retrospective from a former CEO, but because there are 200,000 sitting CEOs who got handed the most consequential job in their company with no manual and no support system.
If I can guide a first-time CEO through her first board meeting this quarter, or help a stagnated CEO see his blind spot that has cost him two great executives this year, that is success to me.
Over four decades in business, I have seen, more times than I care to count, companies with everything going for them fail because of poor leadership from the CEO seat.
These businesses had a real market, a product customers wanted, talented people who showed up ready to do great work—i.e., everything you need for a home run.
If I can help a CEO run their company a little better because of something we worked on together, that's the only kind of legacy I'm interested in anymore.
By that definition, legacy is about whether you are still useful right now, to people navigating the highest-pressure job in business today.
So one reason I am driven to help CEOs understand the job and do it well is that it’s really hard to watch preventable mistakes.
